chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding and testing an idea

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding a problem worth solving
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List problems you have seen in sport and pick one worth solving.
This lesson builds toward: Given problems you have seen in your sport, you will list and rate problems by how many people have them, how painful they are and whether people already pay, then choose one, with the chosen problem one you have seen in real life.
Good business ideas start with a problem, not a product. Athletes see many problems up close: parents who can't find good beginner coaching, teams that lose equipment, players who can't afford quality training, coaches drowning in scheduling.
Write problems you, teammates, parents or coaches complain about. For each, ask: How many people have this problem? How painful is it? Are they already paying for a bad solution?
Use an AI assistant to brainstorm: "I'm a high school volleyball player. List 15 problems players, parents and coaches have that a small business could solve." Then circle the ones you have actually seen.
Step by step:
- Write problems you have seen in your sport.
- Ask AI to brainstorm more.
- Circle the ones you have seen in real life.
- Rate each: how many people, how painful, already paying?
- Pick one.
Words to know:
- Entrepreneur: someone who starts a business to solve a problem.
- Pain point: a problem that bothers people enough that they want it fixed.
Try it now: List five problems from your sport, add more with AI, rate them, and pick the one you will work on.
You can now find and choose a real problem worth solving.

check.q: Which is a sign of a problem worth solving?
options: People are already paying for a bad solution
It is fun to talk about
check.why: If people already pay for a bad solution, the problem matters to them.

check.q: AI lists 15 problems for your sport. What do you do?
options: Circle the ones you have actually seen
Ask AI to pick for you
check.why: Keep the problems you have seen in real life.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Talking to real customers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Interview five potential customers about the problem before building anything.
This lesson builds toward: Given five people who have the problem, you will interview them about past behavior and write down what they say, with no "Would you buy?" questions and the patterns across all five noted.
Before spending money, talk to the people who have the problem. Your goal is to learn, not to sell. Ask about their past behavior, not what they might do someday.
Good questions: "Tell me about the last time this happened." "What did you do about it?" "What did that cost you?" "What's annoying about the options you have?" Avoid "Would you buy my idea?" because people say yes to be nice.
Talk to five people. Write what they say in their words. If most don't care, that is great news: you saved time and money. Pick a new problem or adjust.
Step by step:
- List five people who have the problem.
- Ask about the last time it happened.
- Ask what they did and what it cost.
- Write their words down.
- Look for patterns across the five.
Words to know:
- Customer interview: a short conversation to learn about someone's problem.
- Validate: check that a problem and solution are real before building.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to help you write five interview questions about past behavior. Interview at least two people this week and write down what they said.
You can now interview potential customers to test whether a problem is real.

check.q: What is your goal in a customer interview?
options: To get a promise to buy
check.why: Talk to learn about the problem, not to sell.

check.q: A parent says, "I'd totally buy that someday." What do you ask next?
options: "Tell me about the last time this problem happened."
check.why: Ask about past behavior, since people say yes to be nice.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Shaping your solution and offer
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence solution and the simplest version you could test.
This lesson builds toward: Using what customers told you, you will write a one-sentence solution and choose the simplest test you can run in two weeks, with a number that will show whether the test worked.
Now describe your solution in one sentence: "Saturday beginner basketball sessions for 6-to-9-year-olds, led by high school varsity players, at a price parents can afford."
Start with the simplest test you can run, sometimes called a minimum viable product: one session instead of a full academy, a sign-up form instead of an app, ten shirts instead of 500.
AI can help you think through the simplest version: "Here's my idea and what five customers told me. What's the smallest, cheapest way to test it in two weeks?" Then pick what you can actually do.
Step by step:
- Write your solution in one sentence.
- Ask AI for the smallest test you could run.
- Choose a test you can do in two weeks.
- Decide how you'll know it worked (for example 8 sign-ups).
Words to know:
- Minimum viable product (MVP): the simplest version of your idea that lets you test it with real customers.
- Offer: exactly what customers get and what it costs.
Try it now: Write your one-sentence solution. Use AI to find the smallest two-week test, and write the number that would mean it worked.
You can now describe your solution and design a small, cheap test.

check.q: What is a minimum viable product?
options: The simplest version that lets you test with real customers
check.why: An MVP is the smallest test you can run with real customers.

check.q: You want to start a training academy. What is the best first test?
options: Rent a building for a year
Run one session with a sign-up form
check.why: Start with the simplest test you can do in two weeks.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: A one-page business plan with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page business plan with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Using your notes and an AI assistant, you will write a one-page business plan with problem, solution, customer, what customers said, reach, money and next steps, with invented numbers removed or marked as guesses and feedback from a mentor.
A one-page plan keeps you focused. Sections: Problem, Solution, Customer, What customers told me, How I'll reach them, Money (costs and price), Next steps.
Give an AI assistant your notes and interview results and ask: "Turn these notes into a one-page business plan with these sections. Use plain words. Mark anything that's a guess."
Read it carefully. AI can make your idea sound bigger than it is or invent numbers. Keep only what is true or clearly marked as a guess, and share it with a mentor, coach or teacher for feedback.
Step by step:
- Gather your problem, solution and interview notes.
- Ask AI for a one-page plan with set sections.
- Remove invented numbers or mark them as guesses.
- Share with a mentor for feedback.
Words to know:
- Business plan: a written summary of how a business will work and make money.
- Mentor: an experienced person who gives you advice.
Try it now: Use AI to turn your notes into a one-page plan. Mark every guess, then ask a mentor, coach or teacher for one piece of feedback.
You can now write a one-page business plan with AI and check it for accuracy.

check.q: Which section belongs in your one-page plan?
check.why: The plan includes what your five interviews showed.

check.q: AI's plan says 500 customers in the first month, but you have no evidence. What do you do?
options: Remove it or mark it as a guess
check.why: Keep only what is true or clearly marked as a guess.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Building a start-up budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a simple start-up budget in a spreadsheet.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets, you will build a start-up budget with costs, expected income, totals and profit, with real vendor prices, checked formulas and a review with a trusted adult before spending.
A start-up budget lists what you need to spend before and during your first test, and what you expect to earn. Keep it small at first.
In Google Sheets, list costs (equipment, facility, website or platform fees, printing, insurance if needed, marketing) and expected income (price times expected customers). Find real prices from vendors, not guesses.
Ask AI to set up formulas for totals and profit, and check them yourself. Never borrow money or use a credit card for a business test without talking to a parent, guardian or trusted adviser. This is not financial advice.
Step by step:
- List every start-up cost.
- Look up real prices.
- Estimate income: price times customers.
- Add totals and profit with formulas.
- Review with a trusted adult before spending.
Words to know:
- Start-up budget: a plan of the money needed to start and what you expect to earn.
- Expense: money you spend to run the business.
Try it now: Build a start-up budget for your two-week test in Google Sheets with real prices. Ask AI to write the total and profit formulas and check them.
You can now build a simple start-up budget with real numbers.

check.q: How do you estimate expected income?
check.why: Expected income is price times expected customers.

check.q: Your budget shows you need to buy equipment. What do you do before spending?
options: Put it on a credit card
Review the budget with a parent, guardian or trusted adviser
Buy the cheapest option online now
check.why: Talk to a trusted adult before borrowing or spending on a test.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Rules every athlete-founder checks
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a rules checklist for your business.
This lesson builds toward: Before launching, you will write a rules checklist covering NIL, names and logos, business license, records and taxes, with a USPTO search done and the person you checked each rule with named.
NIL: if your business uses your name, image or likeness, it may count as NIL activity. College athletes may need to report it; Division I athletes report qualifying third-party deals through NIL Go at the time of writing. High school rules vary by state. Ask your compliance office or state athletic association.
Names and logos: do not use school, team or league logos without permission. Before choosing a business name, search the USPTO trademark records and your state's business name records. Your city or state may require a business license; check your local government's website.
Records and taxes: keep every receipt and payment in a spreadsheet. The IRS says you must file a tax return if your net self-employment earnings are $400 or more. Talk with a tax professional. If you are under 18, a parent or guardian will need to help with accounts and contracts.
Step by step:
- Ask compliance or your state association about NIL rules.
- Make sure you use only your own logo and name.
- Search USPTO and state business name records.
- Check local business license rules.
- Set up a receipts and payments sheet.
- Talk with a tax professional.
Words to know:
- Business license: permission from a city, county or state to run a business there.
- Self-employment: earning money from your own business instead of a boss.
Official sources:
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
- USPTO: Trademark basics
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page plan with budget, then write your rules checklist with who you asked about NIL, your trademark search result, your local license check and your records sheet.
You can now check the key rules before launching a business as an athlete.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem and customer The problem is vague or not one the learner has seen. One real problem, rated for size and pain, with a clear customer. Shows what customers already pay for a bad solution. Customer interviews Fewer than five people, or the notes are about whether they would buy. Five interviews about past behavior, written in the customers' words, with patterns noted. The plan changed because of what customers said. One-page plan Sections missing, or invented numbers left unmarked. All seven sections on one page, guesses marked, and mentor feedback received. Includes the two-week test and the number that will show it worked. Start-up budget Guessed prices or formulas not checked. Every cost with a real price, expected income, totals and profit, checked and reviewed with a trusted adult. Shows how many customers are needed to cover start-up costs. Rules checklist NIL, names, license or tax items missing, or no one named. NIL, names and logos, license, records and taxes each listed with who the learner checked with. A USPTO search result and a receipts and payments sheet are attached. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where do you check whether your city requires a business license?
check.why: Your city or state may require a license; check your local government's website.

check.q: You picked a business name. What do you check before using it?
options: USPTO trademark records and your state's business name records
check.why: Search trademark and state business name records before choosing a name.
